newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian premier urges order so aid can come in.
newsitem.headline: Albanian premier urges order so aid can come in.

text.p: Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino appealed on Wednesday for the restoration of order so that humanitarian aid needed to rebuild the battered country can start arriving.
He was speaking only hours after the head of a European Union mission to Albania said the country would have to improve security in the country before the West could offer aid.

Shortly after the premier spoke four army tanks patrolled the main boulevard of Tirana in the strongest show of force in the capital since the new government moved late last week to bring armed unrest in the country under control.

It was not immediately clear what was behind the deployment. The capital has been gradually returning to normal after three days of near-anarchy last week, and the city appeared calm earlier in the day.
On Wednesday morning police moved to secure Tirana airport to reopen Albania's main gateway to the outside world, expected on Thursday.

Fino, appointed only last week, called on behalf of the government for national reconcilation, saying it was committed to its programme for normalising the situation and would guarantee supplies of bread, water and electricity.
He said that in order to enable foreign aid to come in it was necessary to restore the normal functioning of ports, the airport and border posts.

"It is imperative to lay down your arms and keep calm, to work as brothers in support of the government and the country and against those trying to sow chaos and terror," the premier said in an address carried by state television.
The head of an EU mission probing how to help Albania get back on its feet after more than 100 deaths said no infusion of aid was possible until order had been fully restored.

"Our aim is to get aid in as quickly as possible, and we will make a priority list of things that can be done right away," Dutch diplomat Jan de Marchant et d'Ansembourg, the head of the 11-man delegation, told a news conference.

"We are asking Albania to help us help them, they have to create a situation in the country so that the help we give them doesn't fall into the wrong hands. The police are a shambles, there are no prisons, customs or border police and hardly any army, they need just about everything."

Fino, head of the government overseeing elections in June, remained in Tirana on Wednesday, apparently cancelling plans to travel to south to talk to rebels who took control last month and are demanding the resignation of President Sali Berisha.

The unrest was sparked in the south by the collapse of shady investment schemes which soaked up the savings of hundreds of thousands of Albanians. It spread to the north and threatened to engulf Tirana last week before authorities regained control.
On Monday rebel leaders in the south gave Berisha until Thursday to quit, threatening to create an alternative presidential council in the south if he refused.

Italian Chinook military helicopters landed twice on Wednesday at Tirana airport, closed almost a week ago, and Italian paratroopers handed over to Albanian police nearly 300 presumed criminals they said had taken advantage of the unrest to flee across the Adriatic. Many of those arriving denied having committed any crime.

In Italy, the government declared a national "state of emergency", recognising that it had been overwhelmed by a flood of well over 10,000 refugees from Albania in less than a week. Many have made the crossing in barely seaworthy craft.
